'''''Araucaria columnaris''''', the '''coral reef araucaria''', '''Cook pine''' (or '''Cook's pine'''), '''New Caledonia pine''', '''Cook araucaria''', or '''columnar araucaria''', is a species of [[conifer]] in the family [[Araucariaceae]].

==Distribution==
The tree is [[endemism|endemic]] to [[New Caledonia]] in the [[Melanesia]] region of the [[Pacific]].

It was first classified by [[Johann Reinhold Forster]], a botanist on the [[second voyage of James Cook|second voyage of Captain James Cook]] to circumnavigate the globe as far south as possible. It is named directly after Cook, and not from the [[Cook Islands]].

==Description==
''Araucaria columnaris'' is a distinctive narrowly conical tree growing up to {{cvt|60|m|ft}} tall in its native habit. The trees have a slender, spire-like crown.<ref name=gymn/> The shape of young trees strongly resembles ''[[Araucaria heterophylla|A. heterophylla]]''. The bark peels off in thin paper-like sheets or strips and is rough, grey, and resinous.<ref name=gymn/> The relatively short, mostly horizontal branches are in whorls around the slender, upright to slightly leaning trunk. The branches are lined with cord-like, horizontal branchlets. The branchlets are covered with small, green, incurved, point-tipped, spirally arranged, overlapping leaves. The young leaves are needle-like, while the broader adult leaves are triangular and scale-like.<ref name=gymn/>

The female seed cones are scaly, egg-shaped, and {{cvt|10|-|15|cm|in|0}} long by {{cvt|7|-|11|cm|in|0}} wide. The smaller, more numerous male pollen cones are at the tips of the branchlets and are scaly, foxtail-shaped, and {{convert|2|in|cm|0|abbr=in|order=flip}} long.<ref name=gymn/>

A 2017 study found that Cook pine tends to have a tilt dependent on the hemisphere of its location, growing upright on the Equator but leaning south in the northern hemisphere and north in the southern hemisphere.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Johns|first1=J. W.|last2=Yost|first2=J. M.|last3=Nicolle|first3=D.|last4=Igic|first4=B.|last5=Ritter|first5=M. K.|year=2017|title=Worldwide hemisphere-dependent lean in Cook pines|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/317275781|journal=Ecology|volume=98|issue=9|pages=2482–2484|doi=10.1002/ecy.1850|pmid=28556968|bibcode=2017Ecol...98.2482J }}</ref>

==Ornamental tree==
It is cultivated in gardens and public landscapes in [[New South Wales]], [[Queensland]] and [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]] in Australia, northern [[New Zealand]], [[Southern California]], [[Puerto Rico]], [[Mexico]], [[India]], [[Philippines]], [[Hawaii]], [[South Brazil]], [[Singapore]], and [[Southeast Brazil]].<ref name=gymn>{{cite web|url=http://www.conifers.org/ar/Araucaria_columnaris.php| publisher=The Gymnosperm Database|title=Araucaria columnaris}}</ref> Many of the "[[Araucaria heterophylla|Norfolk Island pines]]" that grow in Hawaii, including their descendants used as potted ornamentals on the U.S. mainland, are actually ''A. columnaris'', the two species having been confused when introduced.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pacifichorticulture.org/articles/the-araucaria-family-past-present/ |title=The Araucaria Family: Past & Present |first=Wayne P.|last=Armstrong |publisher=Pacific Horticulture Society |date= |access-date=6 March 2021}}</ref> The stoutest recorded, an ornamental specimen at Ulupalakua, [[Maui]], [[Hawaiʻi]] is only {{cvt|1.2|m}} in [[diameter at breast height]].<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.conifers.org/ar/Araucaria_columnaris.php | last= Earle |first= Christopher J. | title= Gymnosperm Database | date= February 22, 2025 | access-date= May 23, 2025}}</ref>
